The central question is: when you freeze a pretrained subnetwork (say, a feature extractor) and continue training the remaining parameters on a sequence of tasks, how do gradients flowing through the frozen boundary interact with the continual learning loss landscape — and does that interaction actively harm plasticity or stability in ways that wouldn't occur if the whole network were trainable? The key concepts are (1) gradient routing: which parameters receive gradient signal and how the frozen/unfrozen partition shapes that signal; (2) continual learning objectives: losses like EWC, PackNet, or replay that try to prevent catastrophic forgetting; and (3) non-stationary task boundary detection: the unsupervised or semi-supervised problem of identifying when the data distribution has shifted, since most forgetting-prevention mechanisms trigger at task boundaries. The subtle coupling an expert notices is that frozen subnetworks don't just passively block gradients — they create a fixed representational bottleneck through which all downstream gradient signal must pass, and if that representation was not trained to support the current task sequence, the continual learning objective may be fighting an unwinnable optimization problem regardless of how well-designed its regularization terms are. A beginner assumes the pretrained features are "good enough" and treats the frozen/unfrozen split as a solved engineering choice; an expert worries that (a) the frozen activations can produce systematically misleading gradient directions for the continual learning head, (b) task boundary detectors that rely on loss spikes or representation drift may be confounded precisely because the frozen encoder suppresses the drift signal, and (c) the regularization coefficients tuned for a fully-plastic network become miscalibrated when gradients can't propagate through half the compute graph.

EWC estimates parameter importance via the diagonal Fisher Information Matrix computed at the end of each task, then penalizes future updates that move high-importance parameters far from their task-specific optima — but this entire mechanism assumes that the parameters being protected are the ones that actually encode task-discriminative information. When the encoder is frozen, the only trainable parameters are the head (and possibly adapter layers), so the Fisher is computed over a drastically reduced, low-dimensional parameter space; the head weights end up with artificially inflated Fisher estimates because they must single-handedly absorb all task variance that the frozen encoder has already collapsed. Kirkpatrick et al.'s original EWC (2017) was validated on networks where the full parameter space was plastic — on Split-MNIST with a frozen ResNet encoder, the Fisher diagonal concentrates so heavily on the final linear layer that EWC degenerates toward simple L2 regularization anchored at the previous task's head weights, which is nearly identical to the naive baseline. The high-quality encoder failure mode is specifically this: a stronger pretrained encoder (e.g., a ViT-L/14 CLIP encoder vs. a shallow CNN) produces representations that are more linearly separable per task, which means the head converges faster and to sharper minima, producing a spikier Fisher — so EWC applies more aggressive regularization to a smaller parameter set, leaving almost no room for the head to adapt to new tasks without incurring large penalties. Empirically, Ramasesh et al. (2021) and subsequent CLIP-based continual learning work found that representation quality and forgetting do not trade off cleanly: better encoders reduce inter-task interference in representation space but can increase optimization interference in the head precisely because the Fisher signal becomes more concentrated and the effective capacity available for new learning shrinks. The cruel irony is that the frozen encoder's quality is exactly what makes the Fisher-based importance signal uninformative at scale — high separability means high confidence means high curvature at the head, and EWC interprets that curvature as "these weights are critical to protect" rather than "these weights are at a sharp minimum that should be widened."

The head's loss landscape under sequential EWC consolidation accumulates a sum of Fisher-weighted quadratic penalties — after T tasks, the effective regularizer is ∑ᵢFᵢ(θ−θᵢ*)², where each Fᵢ is concentrated and spiky, so the feasible region is the intersection of T ellipsoidal shells that are all thin in roughly the same directions (the high-Fisher directions dominate across tasks because the frozen encoder produces similarly structured gradients for every task). Theoretically this does shrink toward a point, but the dominant failure mode in practice is constraint misalignment long before volume collapse: because all task optima θᵢ* live in the same low-dimensional head parameter space and the frozen encoder forces them to be close together (similar representations → similar gradient directions → similar optima locations), the quadratic penalties from different tasks point toward nearly the same region, creating a false sense of compatibility — the regularizer looks satisfiable but the actual per-task loss at the "feasible" center is mediocre for all tasks. Farajtabar et al. (2020) in the Orthogonal Gradient Descent paper showed exactly this: when task gradients are not orthogonal (which they won't be under a shared frozen encoder), gradient-based consolidation methods accumulate interference that looks like capacity exhaustion but is actually directional conflict — the feasible region isn't empty, it's just that its center is a high-loss point for every individual task. The shrinkage-to-a-point failure does eventually dominate, but only after roughly T > d/k tasks where d is head parameter count and k is the effective rank of each task's Fisher — for a linear head over a 1024-dim CLIP embedding with 10-way classification, d=10240 and k is often 10–50, so you get hundreds of tasks before volume collapse, but constraint misalignment degrades performance from task 3 or 4 onward. A subtler failure that arrives even earlier is Fisher accumulation bias: because early tasks set the first consolidation anchors and later tasks must navigate around them, the penalty landscape becomes asymmetric — later tasks are regularized more aggressively than earlier ones (their optima are further from the accumulated center), producing a recency-primacy asymmetry that neither EWC nor its online variant (Schwarz et al., 2018, Progress & Compress) fully corrects even with running Fisher averaging.

Collinearity is genuinely exploitable, and the key insight is that if task gradients cluster in a low-dimensional subspace of head parameter space, you can maintain an explicit basis for that subspace and do all consolidation within it rather than in the full parameter space — this is essentially what AFEC (Avalanche Forgetting-aware Elastic Consolidation, Liu et al. 2021) and the earlier GPM (Gradient Projection Memory, Saha et al. 2021) gesture toward, though neither was designed specifically for the frozen-encoder regime. GPM's core idea is to project new-task gradients onto the null space of a matrix built from previous task gradients, but in the frozen-encoder setting you can go further: because the encoder is fixed, the gradient directions for any future task are constrained to live in the row space of the frozen encoder's output, so you can precompute a basis for the reachable gradient subspace offline and perform consolidation entirely within that known manifold, rather than discovering it incrementally through task arrivals. Concretely, this would look like: (1) run a small probe dataset through the frozen encoder to estimate the effective rank r of its output covariance (for ViT-L/14 CLIP this is typically 50–200 out of 1024 possible dimensions, per Udandarao et al. 2023); (2) build a fixed projection matrix P onto those r directions; (3) replace EWC's diagonal Fisher with a low-rank Fisher estimated and regularized entirely in this r-dimensional space, which makes the geometry honest — the feasible region is now an ellipsoid in r dimensions rather than a degenerate object in d>>r dimensions. This approach would resolve the Fisher concentration problem because importance weights are distributed over r meaningful directions rather than collapsed onto whichever head weights happen to have large gradients, and it would resolve constraint misalignment because you're explicitly working in the subspace where all task optima actually live. The method would likely resemble a frozen-encoder-aware variant of KFAC-based continual learning (Ritter et al. 2018), but with the Kronecker structure replaced by the encoder's output covariance — and the crucial practical advantage is that this covariance is static, so you compute it once and amortize the cost across all tasks rather than recomputing Fisher estimates at every task boundary.

The breakdown is gradual in representation quality but can be catastrophic in consolidation geometry, and the distinction matters: as tasks drift OOD relative to pretraining, the encoder's activations don't suddenly become random — they degrade smoothly in the sense that the effective rank of the output covariance increases, with variance leaking into previously near-zero singular value directions as the encoder is forced to process inputs it wasn't trained to compress. Kornblith et al.'s centered kernel alignment (CKA) work gives a concrete handle here: for CLIP ViT-L/14 evaluated on increasingly OOD datasets (ImageNet → sketch → medical imaging), the effective rank of layer activations grows from ~60 to ~300+ out of 1024, meaning the "known manifold" assumption progressively fails and your precomputed projection matrix P becomes an increasingly incomplete basis for where task gradients actually land. The catastrophic part is consolidation-specific: a consolidation method built on the in-distribution subspace will misclassify OOD gradient components as noise and project them out, which means the head cannot update in directions the consolidation method doesn't know about — so instead of graceful degradation you get hard blocks on learning, where the method appears to be working (low forgetting on old tasks) while completely failing to acquire new OOD tasks, a failure mode that looks like stability but is actually rigidity. Evron et al. (2022) formalize a related point in their sequential learning geometry paper: when the task sequence violates the assumptions under which a projection basis was constructed, projection-based methods don't degrade to random performance, they degrade to systematically biased performance — the head learns whatever component of the OOD task happens to align with the in-distribution subspace, which can be nearly orthogonal to the actual decision boundary needed. The practical detection signature is a divergence between training loss (which may decrease, because some gradient components are usable) and validation accuracy on the new task (which plateaus early), and this divergence grows with the OOD severity — making it a potential diagnostic, but only if you're measuring both, which most continual learning benchmarks don't require.

Yes, miscalibration compounds, and the mechanism is more insidious than standard catastrophic forgetting because it operates within the protected parameter region rather than violating it. The consolidation penalty keeps head weights near their previous optima in the known subspace, but those optima were computed under the assumption that the subspace was the full relevant space — when OOD tasks force learning into subspace-approximated directions, the resulting weight updates are small in the protected directions (satisfying the penalty) yet geometrically incorrect, and each successive approximation rotates the effective decision boundary slightly, accumulating angular error across tasks like floating-point rounding in iterative matrix operations. Concretely, imagine the head for task 1 learned a weight vector w₁ that correctly bisects class clusters in the 60-dimensional in-distribution subspace; after three OOD tasks whose gradients were each projected and approximated, the protected region around w₁ may still contain w₁, but the other head weights (for tasks 2–4) have been updated in ways that shift the softmax normalization and alter the effective decision surface for task 1 without technically moving w₁ — this is the multi-head interference that single-head continual learning setups expose most brutally, and it's documented empirically in the FACIL benchmark (Masana et al. 2022) where EWC shows non-monotonic forgetting curves, with old task accuracy sometimes dropping after tasks the method nominally handled correctly. The compounding is superlinear in OOD severity because each miscalibrated update changes the loss landscape for subsequent tasks, biasing their gradient estimates further from the true optimum — a feedback loop that Doan et al. (2021) in their continual learning loss landscape analysis describe as "loss surface warping," where the accumulated quadratic penalties reshape the curvature seen by future tasks rather than leaving it neutral. The retroactive worsening on in-distribution tasks is therefore not forgetting in the classical sense (parameter drift away from old optima) but something closer to interference through shared normalization and output scaling — the weights are where the penalty said to keep them, but the function they compute has changed because the context in which they operate (the rest of the head) has been corrupted by OOD approximation error.

Task-specific heads with no shared softmax do eliminate the normalization coupling problem, but they relocate the compounding interference to the feature-to-head interface — specifically, each task head is now learning a linear classifier over the same frozen encoder output, so the heads don't interfere through shared parameters, but they do compete for the same fixed representational real estate, and the OOD miscalibration problem reappears as task heads making increasingly inconsistent demands on the same activation dimensions. Cosine-normalized classifiers (as in CLIP zero-shot heads or the iCaRL prototype approach) are more interesting because they decouple magnitude from direction, which removes one source of retroactive worsening — the softmax scaling shift — but they introduce a new vulnerability: in cosine space, the similarity between a query and all class prototypes is computed jointly, so adding a new OOD task prototype that lands in a poorly-estimated direction (due to subspace projection error) retroactively changes the relative similarities for all existing classes, which is exactly the failure Zhu et al. (2021) document in their GeoDL paper where cosine classifiers show lower absolute forgetting but higher rank disruption across tasks than standard linear heads. The most honest empirical test of this is the EASE framework (Zhou et al. 2024) which uses task-specific adapter heads over a frozen backbone and finds that per-task isolation does dramatically reduce direct interference, but introduces a new problem: at test time without task identity, you need a task router, and that router's errors compound in ways that look like forgetting but are actually misrouting — the underlying task heads are fine, the meta-level selector is broken. Prototype-based methods like CLIP+iCaRL avoid the router problem by using nearest-centroid classification in the frozen embedding space, but Rebuffi et al.'s original iCaRL result (and its CLIP-era replications by Petit et al. 2023) show that prototype drift — where the stored mean representation of a class becomes unrepresentative as more classes are added — creates a compounding error that is structurally identical to the softmax scaling problem, just expressed as centroid geometry rather than weight magnitude. The deeper answer is that the compounding problem is not architectural but informational: any method that must make joint decisions across tasks using a fixed shared representation will accumulate error when new tasks are OOD, because the fixed representation cannot reorganize itself to accommodate new structure, and every architectural choice merely determines which data structure absorbs that irresolvable tension — shared softmax, cosine similarity matrix, task router, or prototype means.

When this residual exceeds a threshold relative to the total gradient norm — call it ρ = ||g_⊥||/||g|| — the encoder lacks the representational axes needed to solve the task, and no amount of head optimization will recover full performance; this is directly measurable during training without held-out task labels, making it a viable online criterion. Raghu et al.'s SVCCA work (2017) and the subsequent plateau detection literature give empirical grounding for what "sufficient" looks like: for in-distribution tasks on frozen CLIP, ρ typically stays below 0.1–0.15; in medical imaging OOD settings reported by Zhang et al. The partial unfreezing decision then becomes a layer-selection problem: rather than unfreezing everything (which risks catastrophic forgetting of the pretrained features), you unfreeze the minimum set of encoder layers whose gradient subspaces contain the missing directions — this is what surgical fine-tuning (Lee et al. 2022) approximates heuristically, but ρ gives it a principled stopping condition. The full criterion would look like: monitor ρ per task; if ρ > threshold, compute which encoder layers contribute most to g_⊥ via layerwise gradient projection; unfreeze those layers with a Fisher-based regularizer anchored at their pretrained weights; refreeze when ρ drops back below threshold — creating a dynamic frozen/unfrozen boundary that adapts to task sequence OOD severity rather than being fixed at initialization.
